chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Safwan — and Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan — all together from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'Does Yahya ibn Sa'id differ from your judges?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Bring me something in which they disagreed.' I said: 'Two youths fought each other in an open space; one of them bit his companion. So the bitten one deliberately picked up a stone and struck with it the head of his companion who had bitten him, splitting it open. He then became afflicted with tetanus and died. That matter was brought before Yahya ibn Sa'id, and he ordered qisas. This was deemed grave by Ibn Abi Layla and Ibn Shubruma, and there was much discussion about it, and they said: This is but an error. So Isa ibn Ali paid the blood money from his own wealth.' He then said: 'Those with us do indeed impose qisas for a deliberate blow; rather, the error is when one intends something but strikes something else.'

key_terms.الدِّيَةُ: Diya — blood money paid as compensation when an act is deemed unintentional or where qisas is waived
key_terms.الرَّحَبَةُ: An open area or courtyard — the setting of the altercation
key_terms.الْخَطَأُ: Error or unintentional act — in Islamic jurisprudence, when someone intends one target but accidentally strikes another; carries blood money (diya) not qisas
key_terms.الْقِصَاصُ: Qisas — the principle of equal retaliation in kind; the Imam affirms it is applicable when the act is deliberate
key_terms.الْوَكْزَةُ: A deliberate, intentional blow or strike — the Imam uses this term to define intentional injury that carries qisas liability, regardless of the instrument

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia ruling on qisas when someone deliberately strikes another causing death — is intentional blow sufficient for qisas even without a lethal weapon?
ai.summary: In this legal hadith, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) engages in a jurisprudential dialogue with his companion Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj about a real legal case that divided early Muslim jurists. The case involved a youth who deliberately picked up a stone and struck his companion's head after being bitten, causing death. Yahya ibn Sa'id — a prominent Sunni jurist and judge in Medina — ruled for qisas (retaliatory execution), while other judges, Ibn Abi Layla and Ibn Shubruma, considered it an error for which only blood money was due. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) affirmed the qisas ruling: a deliberate intentional blow (al-wak'za) warrants qisas regardless of the weapon used; only a case where someone intends one target but accidentally hits another constitutes an error. This hadith illustrates the Shia principle that deliberate intent, not the type of weapon, determines whether an act is homicide or error in Islamic law.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Safwan and Abu Ali Al Ashary, from Muhammad Bin Abdul Jabbar, from Safwan, altogether fro, Abdul Rahman Bin Al Hajjaj who said,

‘Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> said to me: ‘Does Yahya Bin Saeed oppose your judges?’ I said, ‘Yes’. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Give me something from what he differed in’. I said, ‘Two boys fought each other in the open, so one of them bit his companions. So the bitten one deliberated to pick up a stone, so he struck by it the head of his companion who had bitten him. So it split (his head), and (the wound) exacerbated, so he died. So that was raised to Yahya Bin Saeed, so he judged for the retaliation (revenge). 
So that was grievous upon Ibn Abu Layli, and Ibn Shabrama (other judges), and they spoke a lot with regards to it, and they said, ‘But rather, this is an error’. So Isa Bin Ali paid him from his own wealth’. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘From our<sup>asws</sup> (judgement), let there be retaliation for the (fatal) wounding. But rather, the error is when he intended with something, so he hit something else’.
